messages.author: f8897ea5ea72da6f
messages.subject: Recent publication using rworldmap
parts:
We recently published an article in Environmental Resource Letters that has two figures made using rworldmap: http://iopscience.iop.org/1748-9326/8/1/014054. This journal is open access, so everyone should be able to read the article.

We were interested in the effects of CO2 on regional estimates of crop yield (rather than global averages). Some, but not all, models assume a globally uniform effect of CO2 on crop yield because CO2 concentrations are globally uniform. However, CO2  interacts strongly with climate, and climate is highly spatially variable. Thus it is unlikely that the effect of CO2 is globally uniform. Using experimentally determined estimates of interactions effects between CO2 and precipitation and crop species, we show that the regional variability caused by the interaction between CO2  and climate is of the same magnitude as regional variability from climate alone. Furthermore, not including those effects results in substantially different estimates of which countries benefit most from increasing CO2 concentrations. Thus models should try to include these effects. Although we did not calculate any estimates in this study, CO2 also interacts with nitrogen availability and temperature to a degree that is likely of the same order of magnitude as the interaction with precipitation. There are far fewer studies available to determine empirical estimates of those interactions, and there are not readily available global data sets of nitrogen availability. Thus understanding of interactions between CO2   nitrogen and temperature is a key knowledge gap for estimating regional crop yield in the future.

Clearly a map is a good way to show regional effects, and in figures 5 and 7 of the paper we show the relative effect of CO2 on crop production and calorie production for the world. The figures were made using rworldmap and bpy.colors() from the sp library, and I think they turned out quite nicely.
